claims.text: Anthropic states that getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem for long-running tasks spanning hours or days.
Anthropic identifies the core challenge of long-running agents as working in discrete sessions, where each new session begins with no memory of what came before.

Anthropic's two-part solution for the Claude Agent SDK is an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run and a coding agent that makes incremental progress each session while leaving clear artifacts for the next session.

Anthropic found that even Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK, looped across multiple context windows, falls short of a production-quality web app when given only a high-level prompt such as 'build a clone of claude.ai'.
First failure mode: the agent tries to do too much at once (one-shotting the app), runs out of context mid-implementation, and leaves the next session with a half-implemented, undocumented feature.
Second failure mode: after some features are built, a later agent instance sees progress and declares the job done prematurely.
Third failure mode: Claude marks a feature as complete without proper testing.
The initializer agent's session uses a specialized prompt to create an init.sh script, a claude-progress.txt file logging what agents have done, and an initial git commit showing the files added.

The initializer agent is prompted to write a comprehensive feature requirements file expanding the user's prompt; in the claude.ai clone example this contained over 200 features, all initially marked 'failing'.
Each coding agent is asked to work on only one feature at a time, which Anthropic says was critical to curbing the tendency to do too much at once.

Anthropic found the best way to leave the environment clean was to ask the agent to commit progress to git with descriptive messages and write progress summaries to a progress file, which lets the agent revert bad changes and recover working states.
Each coding session begins by reading the git logs and progress files, then reading the features list and choosing the highest-priority feature not yet done.

Each coding session starts by running init.sh to launch the dev server and a basic end-to-end test (in the claude.ai clone, using the Puppeteer MCP to start a chat, send a message and receive a response) to detect a broken state before new work.

Without explicit prompting, Claude tested with unit tests or curl against a dev server but failed to recognize that a feature did not work end-to-end; prompting it to use browser automation and test as a human user greatly improved verification.
Anthropic instructs that features should only be marked 'passing' after careful testing.
Compaction does not always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent, which is why progress files and git history are used alongside it.

Compaction summarizes a conversation nearing the context window limit and reinitiates a new context window with the summary; Anthropic calls it the first lever in context engineering for long-term coherence.

In Claude Code, compaction preserves architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs, and continues with the compressed context plus the five most recently accessed files.

Overly aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later; Anthropic recommends tuning the compaction prompt on complex agent traces, maximizing recall first and then improving precision.
Tool result clearing is described as one of the safest, lightest-touch forms of compaction.

Structured note-taking (agentic memory) has the agent write notes persisted outside the context window, such as a NOTES.md or to-do list, and pull them back in later; it suits iterative development with clear milestones.

Sub-agent architectures let specialized subagents work with clean context windows, exploring with tens of thousands of tokens but returning condensed summaries of often 1,000-2,000 tokens to a lead agent.

Anthropic recommends server-side compaction over SDK compaction for most long-running conversations; the SDK compaction_control parameter is deprecated in the TypeScript and Ruby SDKs and removed in Python v1.0, where server-side compaction is used via the compact_20260112 edit in context_management.

Agent Skills are directories containing a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name and description); only name and description are preloaded into the system prompt, and the body and linked files load progressively as needed, which Anthropic calls the core design principle of skills.
